item.title: Wells Fargo says customers may be liable for unwanted purchases by their AI agents
item.description:
Source: Yahoo Top Stories (World)
Citi Bank, Wells Fargo, Bank of America and JPMorgan Chase have taken steps to limit third-party AI agents from accessing their platforms and services, and others are following suit. The banks’ decisions, first reported by Axios , come amid mounting concern over AI agents taking unwanted actions on behalf of users. Two-thirds of chief information security officers surveyed in financial services and software ranked agentic AI among their top three cybersecurity risks, and more than one-third named it as their top concern, according to a 2026 study by Palo Alto Networks . “We do not permit third-party AI agents or assistants to log into a customer's account or transact directly within our digital banking platforms,” a Citi spokesperson wrote to USA TODAY. Citi customers can authorize agents to “limited, read-only access to their account information with certain Citi-approved open banking providers,” the statement continued. Citi has not seen reports of agents accessing client accounts. “There’s a window of vulnerability where the systems, the banks, the users are all vulnerable to the speed with which AI is being weaponized,” said Andre Durand, founder and CEO of Ping Identity, which sells identity security infrastructure to financial institutions. He cited concern over AI being used to perpetrate fraud and scams at higher levels as well as fear that agents could be compromised or decide to take malicious action on their own. In an October report by Ping , 71% of consumers surveyed reported concern that an AI agent acting on their behalf could misrepresent their personality or values. However, less than a quarter said they refuse to trust AI with any financial transaction, at 22%. Durand said that “the challenge that we're having right now is how can we detect that it is an agent and not a human asking. And if we can detect that it’s an agent not a human, how do we know that the agent is acting on the authority of the human?” Agent restrictions Bank of America, Capital One and four other global banks created a coalition in September to warn that agentic technology is moving faster than industry standards and protections are keeping up. The coalition highlighted the risk that AI shopping agents pose in particular. “When you give the agent your credentials, it is you authorizing the payment. So we’re just trying to work with these companies and with the industry to say, put a human being in the loop,” Bank of America CEO Brian Moynihan told Bloomberg on Oct. 15. “So before you pay, you authorize it, so that we know that you know you’re paying for something.” According to Moynihan, Bank of America is restricting AI agents’ access to consumer deposits and is working with companies to develop protocols on agents. JPMorgan Chase CEO confirmed to Bloomberg last week that JPMorgan Chase is also blocking outside agents from accessing customer-account information. Bank of America and JPMorgan Chase did not immediately respond to a request for comment from USA TODAY. Wells Fargo has also “taken steps to block unauthorized agents from accessing customer accounts,” a bank spokesperson told USA TODAY. According to Wells Fargo’s updated online access agreement , authorized representative or delegate transactions – including transactions of agents – are considered authorized, unless the user explicitly tells the bank they are not authorized and the bank “have had reasonable opportunity to act on your notification.” The agreement is set to take effect on Nov. 24. It includes a section on third-party AI agents in which users agree that they are "solely responsible” for supervising agents, that the bank may act on the instructions of agents and that all transactions taken by authorized representatives such as agents – “including those you did not want or intend” – are considered authorized. “If you permit an AI Agent or other third party access to the Service, you acknowledge that doing so may adversely impact the commercially reasonable security procedures that you've otherwise agreed to, and you accept the risk of such access,” according to the agreement. Durand said he wasn’t aware of specific instances of agents hacking into banks, but added, “I don’t think a lot of stuff is being reported” in regards to agents or AI activity at banks. Alternative options In addition to blocking unauthorized agents from logging in on behalf of clients, Charles Schwab created its own AI assistant , called Charley, which cannot execute trades but can answer questions and complete routine tasks. Schwab CEO Rick Wurster said in an interview with Bloomberg on Oct. 16 that the bank is blocking between “tens and twenties” of attempts by major AI agents to access and manipulate client funds. As AI agent usage grows — Meta reported that Muse grew to 10 million users on Oct. 21 — Durand emphasized the need for better authentication systems. One-time passwords sent to emails are no longer secure enough, he said, because agents often have access to email. “Passkeys and biometrics ensure that the human is the one authenticating, and/or that the human is the one authorizing,” Durand said. Greta Reich covers the artificial intelligence industry for USA TODAY through a fellowship from the Tarbell Center for AI Journalism. Funders do not provide editorial input. This article originally appeared on USA TODAY: ‘Window of vulnerability’: Banks move to restrict AI agent access This article originally appeared on USA TODAY at https://www.usatoday.com/story/money/2026/10/23/banks-move-to-limit-ai-agent-access/92385119007/

item.title: Democrats are favored to flip the House, but Republicans still have a path to victory
item.description:
Source: Yahoo Top Stories (World)
It's crunch time. With less than two weeks to go until the 2026 midterm elections, Democratic and Republican candidates for the U.S. House of Representatives nationwide are making one last push to persuade voters in their districts — and help their party win or retain control of the chamber on Nov. 3. The stakes are high. President Trump has enjoyed complete Republican control of Congress for the first half of his second term. Flipping the House would give Democrats the power to block parts of the president's agenda, investigate his administration and even impeach him (again) . Historically speaking, a president's party almost always loses seats when voters return to the polls to judge his first two years in office. (The average number lost since World War II? Twenty-six .) Sometimes, the backlash is so pervasive that the president's party loses seats across a wide range of competitive districts — a phenomenon known as a "wave" election. But the past doesn't necessarily predict the future, and Republicans have certain advantages today that they didn't have before. Here's what needs to happen for each party to come out on top. Yahoo The races to watch The first thing to know about any House election is that while all 435 congressional districts are technically up for grabs, roughly 80% of those contests (representing about 350 seats) are not considered competitive. House incumbents have always had huge advantages: money and name recognition, mostly. But their head start has only widened in recent years as partisan polarization and redistricting have helped make the vast majority of congressional districts "safe" for one party . These days, incumbents tend to focus more on fending off primary challengers. The general election can be a breeze in comparison. As a result, this year's true battleground is relatively small. According to the nonpartisan Cook Political Report's " race ratings ," just 17 contests are genuine "tossups" at this point. Another 16 "lean Democratic," and 17 "lean Republican." There's also a third competitive category that includes 18 seats where Democrats are the "likely" winners, and 13 seats where the same could be said about Republicans. That's 81 competitive districts — again, out of 435. It's clear from looking at this year's ratings which party is playing more defense and which is playing more offense — and where. Only 30 Democratic seats are considered competitive, and more than half of them (17) are "likely" to remain Democratic, according to Cook. Just five Democratic seats are tossups. Just two are leaning Republican. In contrast, a full 51 Republican seats are considered competitive — and about half of them are tossups (12) or leaning Democratic (12). Geographically, this year's tossups are concentrated in certain kinds of places: Rust Belt districts in states that have swung from party to party in the past (such as Michigan, Pennsylvania and Ohio); Mid-Atlantic suburbs (in states such as New York, Virginia and North Carolina) where Trump has scrambled some of the usual coalitions; and Sun Belt districts (think Florida, Texas, California and Nevada) where Latinos factor heavily. Trump carried many of these areas in 2024 . On Friday, Cook shifted another 19 of its race ratings toward Democrats — part of a pattern that has seen the outlet move a total of 63 race ratings toward Democrats over the last month. "Republicans' path to keeping control of the House has all but evaporated," Cook's House analyst wrote . "Following this latest round of ratings changes, Democrats now are favored outright in the 218 seats they need to win control of the House. In other words, 220 seats are rated either Solid, Likely or Lean Democrat. Republicans, meanwhile, are favored in 198 seats, rated Solid, Likely, or Lean Republican." Overall, the map gives Democrats more pickup options — which means more paths to a House majority. The path to a Democratic House Senate and governor contests can be quirky — more state-specific and personality-driven. But national dynamics tend to play a larger role in shaping the composition of the incoming House. So it's not just a matter of who has more targets on the board. It's that the board itself tends to tilt to one side or the other, taking most of those targets with it. A recent example was the 2010 midterm election, when impatience with America's slow recovery from the 2008 financial collapse and frustration with President Barack Obama's response helped Republicans gain 64 House seats. Beyond the history of midterm backlash against the president's party, Democrats have two big advantages right now. One is that the current Republican majority is so minuscule — just 219 votes to 214, including an independent who caucuses with Republicans — that Democrats only need a net gain of three seats to win back the House. The other is that the board seems to be tilting in Democrats' favor — assuming the polls are right. Surveys suggest there's one underlying factor pulling the national electorate to the left: dissatisfaction with Trump. According to the data journalists at Silver Bulletin , an average of 60% of Americans currently disapprove of how Trump is handling his job vs. 37% who approve. That puts the president's net approval rating at -23% — near his all-time low. Trump is earning even lower marks on voters' top issue this year: the cost of living . Shortly after he returned to office, roughly equal numbers of Americans approved and disapproved of how the president was handling inflation. But today — as tariffs and the Iran war help drive prices up — 71% disapprove and 25% approve . That's a 46-point gap. President Trump arrives to speak at a campaign rally at F&M Bank Arena on Oct. 10, 2026, in Clarksville, Tenn. AP Photo/Alex Brandon Democrats aren't particularly popular. But for the party in power, it may be hard to overcome this level of dissatisfaction with the status quo. That's why, when pollsters ask their so-called generic ballot question — If an election for U.S. Congress were held today, which party's candidate would you vote for in your district? — Americans are currently giving Democrats a substantial lead of more than 9 percentage points , on average. Making matters worse for Republicans, that lead has grown over the last month as swing voters who favored Trump in 2024 — including some Latinos and independents — say they're planning to vote Democratic. To put a 9-point lead in perspective, Democrats were leading by an average of 7.6 points on the generic ballot at this point in 2018, with Trump as president and Republican majorities in the House and Senate. On Election Day, they picked up 41 seats and flipped the House. If the polls are right, Democrats might win control of the House again. The path to a Republican House But are the polls right? Recently, Republicans have pointed to some surprising survey results on the Senate side — including Democratic leads in rural red states such as Iowa , Kansas and Nebraska — to argue that pollsters might be misjudging public sentiment. They're not wrong to say the polls have missed in the past. Polling errors are commonplace; they happen in most elections. But they tend to be random and to change directions from one cycle to another . The Trump era has been a little different. In each of the three presidential contests that Trump himself has competed in, the final average of polls conducted before Election Day underestimated Republicans' performance in the popular vote by an average of 3.8 percentage points, according to data journalist Nate Silver . The theory is that a phenomenon called nonresponse bias — in which Democratic voters are more eager or available to respond to pollsters than Republican voters — might have made Democratic support look stronger than it actually was. Pollsters try to adjust for this by weighting their results — that is, using statistical methods to give less weight to respondents who are overrepresented demographically and more weight to respondents who are underrepresented demographically. But it's difficult to predict in advance who will show up on Election Day. This time around, there are signs that rural Republicans are not responding to pollsters in certain states . Could that mean Republican candidates in those places will outperform their polling? Possibly. But experts say it may also mean that rural Republicans are less supportive of the GOP than they were in 2024 — potentially voting Democratic or staying home on Nov. 3. A voter walks toward his polling place. REUTERS / REUTERS After all, there's been virtually no polling bias toward Democrats in Trump era elections when Trump himself wasn't on the ballot. In fact, the polls since 2016 have overestimated Republican support in midterm elections (by an average of 0.2%) and off-year, special and runoff elections (by an average of 1.3%), according to Silver . Either way, pollsters aren't seeing signs of this rural effect in most states — and even if they were, it might make only a minor dent in Democrats' 9-point national lead . Redistricting is the other Republican advantage. House redistricting efforts typically take place every 10 years, after each new census reveals changes in population distribution. But last summer, Trump successfully pushed GOP legislators in Texas to pass new congressional district boundaries five years earlier than normal to help Republicans win five additional House seats in 2026. This kicked off a tit-for-tat cycle that saw nine states adopt new congressional maps for the midterms — some to benefit Democrats, others Republicans. Now that the dust has settled, Cook projects that Republicans could win nine seats because of redistricting (in Alabama, Florida, Louisiana, North Carolina, Ohio, Tennessee and Texas), while Democrats could win five (in California and Utah). If that plays out, it would net the GOP four seats overall. It's not what Republicans initially hoped to gain from gerrymandering. "We're not gonna win all 13 of those redistricted seats. That's correct. We're not," GOP House Majority Whip Tom Emmer of Minnesota told Axios recently . But it's also not nothing. The hope for the GOP is that some combination of polling error and redistricting boost — along with a late influx of hundreds of millions of dollars to help defend districts Trump won in 2024 — will be just enough to preserve their slim House majority. item.title: The U.S. has reportedly relied on Elon Musk to help shape foreign policy for years
item.description:
Source: Yahoo Top Stories (World)
By Erin Banco and Joey Roulette WASHINGTON, Oct 23 (Reuters) - Well before the throttling this month of Ukraine's military access to Elon Musk's satellite communications system, the Biden and Trump administrations had several times asked SpaceX to turn its Starlink service on or off in various countries, according to six former senior US officials familiar with the matter. During the presidency of Joe Biden, the requests included switching off the service to prevent Iranian proxy militias in Yemen and Lebanon from using Starlink to communicate, and ‌activating the service to provide internet access inside Iran and in Ukraine to support its military, said four of the former officials. Similarly, President Donald Trump's administration asked Musk, who is CEO of SpaceX, to make the service available in Iran following US-Israeli strikes in ‌2025 and 2026, in hopes it would bolster internet access and communications for anti-government protesters, a former senior Trump official and a person familiar with the matter told Reuters. All of the people spoke on condition of anonymity. The previous US requests about Starlink access are being reported here for the first time. The recent blowup over restrictions to Ukraine's use of SpaceX satellite services ​has raised questions about the ties between the US government and Musk, whose company owns systems vital to the US military and to US allies. The Biden-era and Trump requests to Musk show a close relationship in which US administrations rely to an unprecedented degree on a private-sector company to help implement foreign policy. The recent limits on Ukraine, despite being a US ally, have also rattled officials in Europe, some of whom argue that Europe must develop its own military satellite communications capabilities because no viable short-term alternative currently exists. STARSHIELD RESTRICTIONS HOBBLE UKRAINE MILITARY Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskiy said last week that his country's access to Starshield, the military version of the Starlink system, had been intentionally limited, interfering with the performance of the country’s military drones. He also said the speeds were reduced for Starlink, which Ukraine uses for some military activities including defense against Russian missile attacks. Reuters has reported that the order to throttle Starshield came from inside the White House. The ‌Trump administration has acknowledged the slowdown but has not said whether it gave the order. The White House, contacted ⁠for comment, referred Reuters to Trump's remarks on Friday, when he said he had not spoken with Musk about Starlink access issues for Ukraine and that "if there is a problem, I'll get it straightened out." Halyna Yusypiuk, a spokesperson for the Ukrainian embassy in Washington, said Ukraine's priority is "to have the service restored to normal speed as soon as possible, as the lives of our people depend on it." SpaceX did not respond to requests for comment, although Musk said in ⁠a social media post earlier this week: “Starshield systems are owned and controlled by the US government. Any limits on speed or usage are decided by the US military and ultimately (by the president of the United States).” Democratic US Representative Jason Crow called on Friday for clarity about the recent changes to Ukraine's satellite service, saying there are risks to the US dependence on SpaceX. "Unelected billionaires and private corporations should not decide what is in the best interest of America's national security," Crow said. For Ukraine, the Starlink internet service has become the lifeblood of frontline communication between units, who say there is currently no rival to the capabilities of SpaceX's products. Starshield receivers, largely impervious to radio ​jamming, ​are used as onboard guidance systems and to provide links to a remote pilot for Ukrainian drones, including deep behind Russian lines inside Ukraine. MUSK'S INFLUENCE RAISES UNCERTAINTY Musk's role ​as the strong-willed CEO of a company with outsized influence over US national security has at times raised questions ‌over who is making decisions about SpaceX's satellite services. The SpaceX CEO is "supposed to be a business executive, with government contracts, and he's essentially making huge foreign policy decisions," said Armand Musey, president of Summit Ridge Group, a satellite industry consultancy. "He's sufficiently ambiguous of a person that you don't know if his decisions are sort of his personal quirks, or it's because there's an influence elsewhere that's impacting him," Musey said. In previous years, Musk has moved to limit Ukraine’s access to Starlink. In 2022, according to Reuters reporting, Musk ordered SpaceX personnel to cut Starlink coverage in areas Ukraine was trying to retake, a move that surprised White House officials. Musk has said publicly that he refused a 2022 Ukrainian request to activate his satellite network in Crimea's port city of Sevastopol to aid an attack on Russia's fleet there, saying he feared complicity in a major act of war. The Biden administration at times relied on Musk to help implement policy, five of the former officials said. Biden officials coordinated with SpaceX to thwart US adversaries by cutting the service, and to help allies by expanding Starlink’s availability, they said. They added that discussions between the government and SpaceX, which usually included Pentagon and White House officials, often focused on ‌preventing groups such as the Iranian-linked Houthis in Yemen and Hezbollah in Lebanon from using Starlink terminals. Biden officials several times shared intelligence with SpaceX that indicated that the Houthis ​and Hezbollah were using diverted Starlink terminals — hardware that made its way to the militants through intermediaries. In October 2023, during fighting between Israel and Hezbollah militants in southern Lebanon, intelligence ​officials told the White House that individuals linked to Hezbollah could have gained access to Starlink terminals. Officials had similar concerns about the ​Houthis in Yemen in 2024 during a US air campaign against the Iran-linked group, five of the officials said. In both cases, the administration contacted SpaceX and asked it to identify the terminals and shut them off. At least some of ‌the terminals were deactivated, said two of the officials. In a 2024 submission to the US Commerce Department's Bureau ​of Industry and Security, SpaceX said it works closely with US government agencies to ​secure export authorizations where required and to safeguard technology in support of US national security objectives and foreign policy goals. Soon after Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022, Biden officials pushed SpaceX to expand Starlink use for the Ukrainian military, said two of the former officials. In a separate instance, the Biden administration asked SpaceX to turn on Starlink in Iran during a protest movement launched in September 2022 after the death of Mahsa Amini, an Iranian arrested for not wearing her hijab properly, according to one of the former officials. Starlink terminals were ​moved into the country with the help of the administration, said the official, who declined to say how many ‌were transferred. The Trump administration took a similar step earlier this year and discussed with Musk and SpaceX getting Starlink terminals into Iran and activated following US-Israeli strikes in the country in June 2025 and again in February 2026, a former senior Trump ​official and a person familiar with the matter told Reuters. Neither the Trump administration nor SpaceX has publicly confirmed that those terminals were turned on. The Wall Street Journal reported in February that the US government had sent thousands of Starlink terminals into Iran. Iran's ​delegation to the UN did not respond to a request for comment. (Reporting by Erin Banco and Phil Stewart; Editing by Don Durfee and Edmund Klamann) This article originally appeared on Reuters at https://www.yahoo.com/news/us/articles/exclusive-us-years-asked-musk-004340637.html

item.title: Trump says noncitizen voting is a threat. A New York woman's arrest complicates the picture.
item.description:
Source: Yahoo Top Stories (World)
An upstate New York woman who says she only recently learned she wasn’t born in the U.S. has been charged with voting illegally, one of the latest arrests touted by the Trump administration as it hunts for noncitizen voters ahead of the midterm elections. Marva Cook was adopted as a toddler and had always assumed she was a U.S. citizen, she told Homeland Security investigators earlier this month, according to the criminal complaint. But in searching for her biological mother, the 66-year-old Syracuse resident, who starred on Syracuse University’s women’s basketball team decades ago, said she discovered she had a German birth certificate. Federal prosecutors say Cook has had a green card for several years now, but she still cast ballots in recent elections despite not having citizenship. She faces a single federal charge of voting by an alien stemming from her vote in the 2022 midterms. The misdemeanor offense carries a maximum sentence of one year in prison and a fine up to $100,000, if convicted. Cook can also face deportation, under federal law . Cook says she has faith in God and support from community Reached by phone Friday, Cook declined to discuss the criminal case, her voting record or her past efforts at becoming a citizen. But she said she was “not thrilled” by her court appearance Wednesday as she was placed in shackles despite having voluntarily turned herself in just hours earlier. “It was a difficult time,” Cook said. “I’m about kindness and service and doing for others as I want to be treated.” She also said she appreciated the outpouring of support of community members, a number of whom accompanied her to court Wednesday. “The prayers and the support is a big part of how I will get through this,” Cook said. “I have a deep faith that God will get me through it.” Cook’s lawyer, Paul Tuck, also declined to discuss details of the criminal case Friday other than to say there are no upcoming hearings or filing deadlines. There are no pending immigration proceedings, he added, but Cook has an immigration lawyer in the event that changes. Spokespersons for the U.S. Department of Homeland Security and U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement didn’t immediately respond to emails seeking comment. Cook is latest arrest in Trump’s nationwide crackdown on noncitizen voting First Assistant U.S. Attorney John A. Sarcone III, whose upstate New York office is prosecuting the case, said Cook's arrest showed “voter fraud is rampant” in the state. Other federal agencies amplified the statement on social media, even as the administration’s own investigations have demonstrated that such instances are incredibly rare and been shown not to change the outcome of elections. “We cannot and will not allow the votes of American citizens to be canceled out by noncitizens illegally voting in our elections,” the Homeland Security wrote in a post on X that included Sarcone's statement. In California, federal authorities on Monday charged more than two dozen legal permanent residents with illegally casting ballots or registering to vote. Weeks earlier, 10 people were charged in Minnesota with illegally voting over the last three elections. Supporters say Cook is a valuable member of the community Cook’s supporters, meanwhile, described her as a vital part of the local community where she had lived nearly all of her life and had starred in college basketball. The Syracuse University athletics department confirmed Cook was the team’s leading scorer in the 1979-80 season, averaging 15 points per game. She also holds the school record for most steals in a single season. Fred Daley, pastor at All Saints Church, said Cook is an active member of the parish who for years has been the church’s go-to Easter Bunny, decked out in full costume during the spring holiday season. “If the government wanted to make a case, they chose the wrong person,” he said. “She’s a poster child of an amazing person. She’s highly respected throughout the community.” Dale Avers, a parishioner who has known Cook for almost 20 years, described her as a “person of service” who “never sought limelight.” She said Cook supports low-income families and youth as the YMCA’s community school program director. “I’m in total shock that they’re putting this much effort into this,” Avers said. “They understood the story. There was no intent. There’s no malice. There was no deception involved.” This article originally appeared on Associated Press at https://www.yahoo.com/news/us/articles/york-state-woman-charged-voting-210057822.html

item.title: DOJ gives California counties 48 hours to help identify suspected noncitizen voters
item.description:
Source: Yahoo Top Stories (World)
Los Angeles (AP) — Federal prosecutors sent letters to county registrars across California on Friday demanding that local officials set aside and verify ballots that the Department of Justice said may belong to noncitizens , according to the Los Angeles County registrar and a letter obtained by The Associated Press. The letters are the latest escalation in a legal battle between California and President Donald Trump's Department of Justice, which has recently focused on the state in its efforts to root out noncitizen voting ahead of the midterm elections. Data shows illegal voting by people who aren't U.S. citizens is incredibly rare , difficult to prove and has not been shown to change the outcome of races. Earlier this month, the federal government targeted Los Angeles County and the California Secretary of State's office in a lawsuit that aimed to block them from counting the votes of roughly 20,000 people who are “likely” noncitizen voters. A hearing on the case is scheduled for Tuesday. The Trump administration asked the 9th Circuit court of appeals to rule on the lawsuit barring a decision from the district judge assigned to the case. They set a deadline for Saturday. Now, according to the LA County registrar’s office, at least 18 counties across the state have received similar letters. They have been given a 48 hour deadline to provide identifying information corresponding with ballots that the federal government believes were sent to noncitizens illegally registered to vote. The letter requests that county officials also sequester any ballots where citizenship cannot be verified. “Any election official who knowingly processes the ballot of a noncitizen is opening themselves to legal jeopardy," said First Assistant U.S. Attorney Bill Essayli. The Justice Department is asking counties to send information about the voters it suspects are noncitizens including social security numbers, ID information, a copy of their registration and more. That information can help the government and state quickly assess each person suspected of illegally registering to vote, said the letter sent to San Bernardino County voting officials. The letter says the government's list of suspected noncitizen voters includes 1,133 people from the inland Southern California county. California’s secretary of state and the Los Angeles County registrar have opposed the federal government’s demands. In legal filings, lawyers for California say the request threatens to delay the certification of the vote and undermine the legitimacy of the November midterms. They have also argued that the federal government's data is unreliable and that their demands risk disenfranchisement of citizens. Voting is underway in California, with the state's more than 23 million registered voters receiving ballots in the mail earlier this month. The state said in legal filings that over 330,000 mail-in ballots have already been counted. The letters on Friday came on the heels of statewide sweep by federal authorities earlier in the week, where 28 people from the list of 20,000 were charged with illegally registering to vote. Some were also charged with illegally voting and lying on naturalization paperwork. Those charges could lead to years in prison. item.title: Philippines investigating abuse allegations against Meghan Markle's father
item.description:
Source: Yahoo Top Stories (World)
FILE PHOTO - Meghan Markle, the Duchess of Sussex, meets volunteer first responders from the Bondi Surf Bathers' Life Saving Club during a visit to Sydney's Bondi Beach. (is associated with: «Philippines investigating allegations against Meghan's father») Jonathan Brady/PA Wire/dpa Authorities in the Philippines said they are investigating allegations that Thomas Markle Sr, the father of Meghan Markle, wife of Britain's Prince Harry, had a hoard of child sex abuse images. According to The Sun, Meghan’s half-brother, Thomas Markle Jr, alleged that he found a stash of images belonging to their father at his former home in the Philippines. He reportedly told police in the country that he discovered the child abuse pictures and videos mixed up with innocent family mementos. The newspaper said he also contacted FBI investigators in the US in July. Nicholas Ty, undersecretary for the Philippines Department of Justice, told ITV News: “Our Anti-Trafficking and Online Sexual Abuse and Exploitation of Children taskforce in Cebu is currently investigating the matter.” In an interview with the Daily Mail, Thomas Sr denied possessing child sex images, calling the accusations “sick lies.” On Friday, Meghan said she was made aware of “disturbing allegations” about her father in 2018. She said she was shown a letter sent to Scotland Yard eight years ago making “troubling” allegations against Thomas Markle Sr and she was assured that these were being investigated. It is understood the Metropolitan Police has not previously, nor is the force currently, investigating Mr Markle. The force said it is making internal inquiries regarding officers from the Met’s Royalty and Specialist Protection Command being involved in the passing on of a letter. The FBI said in a statement: "The FBI is aware of the allegations and will provide support, as appropriate, to the Philippine authorities. "We will also investigate any related allegations of federal violations of US law." It is unclear what the nature of the allegations in 2018 were and whether they are linked to the accusations raised by his son now in 2026. It is understood the letter sent to the Metropolitan Police was shared with Meghan in the summer of 2018, after her wedding to Harry. Meghan became estranged from her former TV lighting director father in the run-up to her 2018 royal wedding after he was caught staging paparazzi photographs. Mr Markle did not attend the wedding, leaving the King to accompany Meghan down the aisle and meaning the only member of her family present was her mother, Doria Ragland. Meghan was the only child of Mr Markle’s marriage to Ms Ragland, though he has two children – Samantha and Thomas Jr – from an earlier marriage. In 2021, Meghan won a High Court privacy and copyright claim against Associated Newspapers Limited (ANL) over articles that reproduced parts of a “personal and private” handwritten letter she wrote to Mr Markle in a bid to get him to stop talking to the press. She penned the emotional five-page letter to him in August 2018 after taking advice from two unnamed senior royals. In 2025, Mr Markle moved to the Philippines for a new life after suffering a series of strokes. Then, in December of that year, he had his leg amputated during life-saving surgery. Meghan “reached out” to him in the aftermath of the operation, a spokesperson for the duchess revealed, and Meghan was also said to have tried to do so previously. He is reportedly now living in a rehab centre in Florida, where he is learning to walk again. Buckingham Palace and the Philippine Department of Justice have been contacted for comment. item.title: Bolsonaro and Lula clash on living costs, corruption in final Brazil election debate

item.title: Hitler's Eagle's Nest retreat engulfed in flames as police detain suspect
item.description:
Source: Yahoo Top Stories (World)
More than 200 firefighters are at the scene in Bavaria - Getty Images Police have detained a suspect after a fire destroyed Adolf Hitler ’s German mountain retreat. Around 200 firefighters were deployed to tackle the fire engulfing the Eagle’s Nest, a remote residence at the top of Obersalzberg mountain in Bavaria built in the 1930s for the Nazi leader. Authorities on Saturday said the building had been almost completely destroyed and that it was unclear whether parts could be salvaged. Police said firefighters had found the building “completely ablaze” as they approached the Kehlsteinhaus residence. Emergency services arrived on site at 9.52pm (8.52pm UK time) after a smoke detector triggered a fire alarm. Flames engulfed the Kehlsteinhaus, known as the Eagle’s Nest, on Friday night - Getty/Ferdinand Dorfler-Farthofer Several hours later, firefighters were struggling to extinguish the fire because of the house’s remote location, police said. A police spokesman said a “suspicious person” had been “taken into temporary custody” but that the criminal investigation was ongoing and that no one had been injured. Hitler’s former retreat is at an altitude of 6,000ft in Obersalzberg - AFP/Getty Images German media reported that no one had been inside the building at the time of the fire, which had been burning for more than 12 hours. Bild reported that authorities arrested a motorcyclist they had encountered as they arrived at the scene. The outlet added that the historic building was probably beyond saving. The residence is at an altitude of 6,000ft (1,834m), making it difficult for firefighters to access, police said. Emergency services at the site in the early hours of Saturday morning - Florian Scherer/Reuters Lisa Maier, a spokesman, said the building was only accessible with “heavy breathing apparatus”. She said police would hold a news conference later on Saturday. Firefighters were also hampered by the narrow road that connects the house to Obersalzberg, which is usually closed to cars. The Italian foreign minister, left, visited Hitler at the Eagle’s Nest in 1939 - Getty/Galerie Bilderwelt The Kehlsteinhaus, nicknamed the Eagle’s Nest, was built to host dignitaries and is located close to the Berghof, Hitler’s summer residence. Workers were forced to labour through the night in the winter of 1938 to complete the building in time for Hitler’s birthday in April 1939. The lavish interior featured a red Italian marble fireplace given by Benito Mussolini, the Italian dictator, which was damaged by Allied soldiers, who chipped off pieces to take as souvenirs. The residence’s altitude and remoteness made it difficult for firefighters to access it - KERSTIN JOENSSON / AFP via Getty Images The dictator visited the Eagle’s Nest at least 14 times, with the house largely used to entertain foreign guests and diplomats. After the Second World War, the house was used by the Allies as a command post until 1960 when it was given back to the state of Bavaria and classified as a historical monument. item.title: Judge rules Jane Doe in Cornell case can remain anonymous while pursuing lawsuit
item.description:
Source: Yahoo Top Stories (World)
A judge in New York on Friday decided the former Cornell University student known as Jane Doe can pursue her sexual assault claim against the university and seven fraternity members while remaining anonymous. Permission to proceed in litigation under a pseudonym is not automatic, but the judge said "the notoriety of the allegations and widespread reports of certain malicious actors' behavior" warranted anonymity. Jane Doe says she felt 'unsupported and disbelieved' by Cornell president The judge's decision came with a warning to those who have threatened Jane Doe and others connected to the case. "While the Court is cognizant that some members of the public have made it their mission to try and identify Jane Doe, and have likewise tried to use what they believe to be Jane Doe's identity to harass and threaten certain individuals allegedly tied to her, the Court issues the following words of caution: cyberstalking and engaging in or encouraging threats across state lines, whether it be of Jane Doe, any of the named defendants, or their attorneys, can be considered a federal crime and perpetrators of those acts may be subjecting themselves to prosecution," Judge Phaedra Perry-Bond wrote in her opinion. Anna Moneymaker/Getty Images - PHOTO: A hand written sign is seen before a rally in support of a former Cornell University student known as Jane Doe at the Ithaca Commons, October 13, 2026 in Ithaca, New York. Former Cornell fraternity president dropped from Jane Doe lawsuit Jane Doe filed a civil lawsuit alleging she had been drugged and gang-raped at the Chi Phi fraternity house in October 2024. All seven men named in the lawsuit have denied wrongdoing and no criminal charges have been filed in the case. Her attorney, Thomas Giuffra, has previously told ABC News that Jane Doe and her family have been subjected to threats, doxxing and other forms of harassment. New York Attorney General Letitia James, who was appointed by Gov. Kathy Hochul, is conducting an investigation into the incident. Cornell, which said it fully supports the appointment of a special prosecutor, is also conducting an internal probe of its response to the allegations. The case has rocked the university and started conversations about treatment of sexual assault allegations on college campuses across the country. Cornell has said it takes allegations of allegations of sexual violence "extremely seriously" and that it "investigated and adjudicated the allegations consistent with university policies." At the same time, the university has said it is committed to taking additional steps to improve campus safety. item.title: U.S. intelligence warns Iranian plots to kill Americans are in 'advanced stages'
item.description:
Source: Yahoo Top Stories (World)
Director of National Intelligence Jay Clayton warned Friday that Iran has "substantially increased efforts to target U.S. personnel" abroad, with plots to kill Americans reaching "advanced stages" in the Middle East and other countries. The warning, contained in an unclassified memo that was sent to Secretary of State Marco Rubio and obtained by CBS News, comes as the State Department adjusts staffing at diplomatic posts across the Middle East , and the U.S. military pares back its footprint in the region, amid concerns about direct threats from Iran and threats from the Iranian-backed Houthi movement in Yemen. "The lethal plotting efforts by the Iranians against U.S. citizens have reached advanced stages in both the Middle East and certain other countries," Clayton wrote. The memo, which was issued as the Trump administration weighs resuming military strikes against Iran, does not identify specific targets or countries where the alleged plots are underway, or indicate whether attacks may be imminent. Clayton said the U.S. intelligence community is working to downgrade sensitive intelligence — received through various channels — so it can be shared more broadly with State Department personnel. CIA Director John Ratcliffe was copied on the memo. Axios was first to report on the memo. The warning follows a series of precautions at U.S. diplomatic facilities across the region. Earlier this week, the State Department ordered non-essential U.S. embassy personnel and their families to depart Saudi Arabia. Several other American embassies in the region adjusted their staffing under "restricted operations" status, which allows them to reduce the number of personnel without formally going on ordered departure, CBS News previously reported. "When it comes to our staffing at embassies, we constantly evaluate new information about the security environment," a U.S. official told CBS News on Friday. "The threat of Houthi attacks and of Iranian terror plots targeting U.S. officials are informing our decisions on staffing adjustments for embassies on RO [Restricted Operations] Status in the region." A U.S. official and a senior U.S. military official also told CBS News this week that the military has been quietly reducing its footprint at posts in the Middle East due to ongoing threats. Houthi militants have stepped up drone and missile attacks against Saudi Arabia, targeting oil infrastructure and airports. One strike on Riyadh's King Khalid Airport earlier this month killed at least a dozen people , including a U.S. citizen, and injured hundreds more. Last weekend, U.S. embassies in Saudi Arabia, Bahrain, Qatar, the United Arab Emirates and other countries warned Americans to exercise caution due to Houthi attacks. Although the U.S. and Iran have refrained from striking each other in recent weeks, President Trump has not ruled out restarting hostilities after next month's midterm elections. Iran has also continued to take responsibility for attacks on oil tankers in the Strait of Hormuz. At a campaign rally in Florida on Friday, Mr. Trump suggested the U.S. could launch another operation against Iran if Tehran failed to reach an agreement. "We may do another little Epic Fury, or they'll agree," the president said, invoking the name of the U.S. military campaign launched in February. item.title: Employee error blamed for toxic chemical leak that sent 60 people to hospital in Ohio
item.description:
Source: Yahoo Top Stories (World)
A chemical leak that sent 60 people to the hospital and forced hundreds of people to flee their homes has been blamed on an employee error. Mayor Wade Kapszukiewicz announced the cause of the tank leak at a news conference on Friday and said that all remaining evacuation orders in Toledo , Ohio . The chemical leak happened Tuesday night when an employee of MC Tank Transport “introduced a temperature level to the tank in the process of trying to transfer the liquid" that caused a chemical reaction, the mayor said. MC Tank Transport said the tank contained glycidyl methacrylate , which it described as “an industrial chemical used to make certain plastics, paints and coatings perform better.” A plume of smokes rises from MC Tank Transport Inc., where a chemical tank exploded overnight, prompting hundreds of residents to evacuate or shelter in place amid concerns about a potential toxic release, Wednesday, Oct. 21, 2026 (AP) The evacuation orders were lifted after the company finished venting the tank that ruptured. That allowed a hazmat team to enter the site and test safety levels. “At this time, we do feel confident that the site is safe," Toledo Fire and Rescue Battalion Chief Blake Molnar said. Dr Brian Kaminski, vice president of medical affairs for ProMedica hospitals, said about 60 patients were treated at the hospital, most suffering relatively minor symptoms. A small number of patients who had underlying health conditions were admitted, he said, and all patients were expected to recover. The company has “accepted responsibility” for what happened, the mayor said. The U.S. EPA on the scene near MC Tank Transport Inc. (AP) “There was no fire, there was no explosion. There was a very serious chemical reaction, which now happily has run its course, and we’re now finally able to return to some level of normalcy here in our community," he said. Based on data that officials have seen so far, the amount of the chemical in the air didn't reach levels high enough to have “a long-term meaningful impact on human health,” according to Kapszukiewicz.
